design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (Review Manager 4.2.2) of randomized and controlled clinical trials comparing Community Reinforcement and Family Training (CRAFT) with Al-Anon/Nar-Anon-based approaches or the Johnson Institute intervention for concerned significant others (CSOs) of adults with substance use disorders who refused treatment. Five databases searched in November 2008; four RCTs included (Sisson & Azrin, 1986; Miller et al., 1999; Kirby et al., 1999; Meyers et al., 2002), 264 CSOs. Outcomes: the relative's entry into treatment (at least one session), pooled as relative risk with numbers needed to treat; and CSO functioning, pooled as change from baseline to 6 months within the CRAFT arms of two trials. Evidence graded with a four-level rating system.
can_establish: The pooled relative chance that a relative who refused treatment entered it when the family member was trained in CRAFT rather than in a twelve-step family approach, across four small US trials published 1986–2002, three of them from CRAFT's originators.
cannot_establish: Whether CRAFT improves family members' own wellbeing compared with no help or with the other approaches (the CSO analysis pools before-and-after scores within CRAFT arms only); whether CRAFT beats the Johnson intervention beyond a single trial; effects on substance use, safety or violence (not synthesized); or effects outside the US and outside trials run by CRAFT's developers.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, PsycINFO, EMBASE, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library in November 2008, using the keywords of an earlier review by the first author plus CRAFT-related terms (Fig 1 legend), with reference checking and author consultation (pp. 1730–1731). Included trials: Sisson & Azrin (1986), 12 female CSOs of male drinkers, 3-month follow-up; Miller et al. (1999), 130 CSOs of people with alcohol problems, 6 months; Kirby et al. (1999), 32 CSOs of people using illicit drugs, mainly cocaine and heroin, 10 weeks; Meyers et al. (2002), 90 CSOs of people using illicit drugs, 6 months (Table 1, p. 1732).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: RCTs or controlled clinical trials comparing CRAFT with Al-Anon/Nar-Anon and/or the Johnson Institute intervention; CSOs of treatment-resistant people aged 18 or older with substance use disorders; therapists trained in the approach and supervised regularly; the primary goal of getting the relative to attend at least one treatment session (pp. 1730–1731). Of 218 records, 109 were excluded as not relevant and 105 as potentially relevant but ineligible (86 on the community reinforcement approach, 13 reviews or discussions, 2 CRAFT book discussions, 3 not RCTs or controlled trials, 1 with other outcome measures) (Fig 1, p. 1730). No language or date limits are stated.
sample.demographics: CSOs in the included trials were 88–100% women, aged 19–81; ethnicity reported for three trials (Anglo 48–75%; Hispanic 39–50% in the two New Mexico trials; African American 22% in Kirby et al.); relationships mostly partners or spouses, with 30–53% parents in three trials (Table 1, p. 1732).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the trials is not reported in the review.
sample.selection_effects: Four small US trials. Two (Miller et al., 1999; Meyers et al., 2002) come from the group that developed CRAFT, and one (Sisson & Azrin, 1986) from the originators of the community reinforcement approach. Comparators differ (Al-Anon facilitation therapy; Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches) and follow-up ranges from 10 weeks to 6 months. Uncontrolled CRAFT studies discussed later in the review were not eligible. The authors thank three authors of included trials for assistance and supplementary data (Acknowledgements, p. 1737).

exposure.measurement: CRAFT (including its earlier form, community reinforcement training) delivered to family members by trained therapists, against Al-Anon/Nar-Anon-based approaches (four trials) or the Johnson Institute intervention (one trial). The content, number of sessions and delivery of each intervention are not described in the review.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (psychosocial intervention for family members). The review states that engagement typically followed four to six CRAFT sessions (p. 1735).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol and illicit-drug trials were pooled; the authors justify this by the overlap of alcohol and drug use and the absence of heterogeneity (Limitations, 2nd paragraph, p. 1735). Substance shares for relatives who did not enter treatment came from family members' reports (Table 1 note).

comparison.controls: Twelve-step family approaches (Sisson & Azrin: Al-Anon model; Miller et al.: Al-Anon facilitation therapy; Kirby et al. and Meyers et al.: Nar-Anon) and, in one trial, the Johnson Institute confrontational intervention. No included trial had an untreated group; the CSO-functioning analysis compares baseline with 6 months within CRAFT arms.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level (randomized trials).

outcomes.instruments: Engagement: the relative attended at least one treatment session (inclusion criterion iv, p. 1731), as defined in each trial. CSO functioning: depression (Beck Depression Inventory), anger, family cohesion, relationship happiness and family conflict, as reported by the trials (p. 1733).
outcomes.validity_norms: Trial quality was scored by two reviewers independently on 11 internal-validity criteria adapted from Cochrane Back Review Group guidelines, 'high quality' meaning six or more criteria met; agreement 84% (κ = 0.65). The criteria and each trial's scores are not listed; all four trials scored six or more (pp. 1731).
outcomes.operationalization: Engagement as a binary outcome pooled as relative risk with numbers needed to treat; family-member 'improvement' as the weighted mean difference between baseline and 6-month scores in the CRAFT arms of two trials; strength of evidence graded on a four-level scale (strong: consistent findings in multiple high-quality RCTs; limited: one RCT) (p. 1731).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Seven pooled estimates: engagement against Al-Anon/Nar-Anon and against the Johnson intervention, and five family-member measures.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Whether study selection and data extraction were done in duplicate is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Engagement, CRAFT vs Al-Anon/Nar-Anon (4 trials; 125 vs 99 CSOs): 84 of 125 (67%; 95% CI 58.97–75.43) vs 18 of 99 (18%; 10.58–25.78); RR 3.25 (95% CI 2.11–5.02), P < 0.0001, NNT 2; Q = 3.09, df = 3, P = 0.38, I² = 2.9% (Fig 2, p. 1733). Trial RRs: Sisson & Azrin 9.75 (0.67–141.44), Miller et al. 4.83 (2.22–10.50), Kirby et al. 3.86 (1.28–11.64), Meyers et al. 2.34 (1.31–4.16). Without Sisson & Azrin: RR 3.21 (1.99–5.17), I² = 15.3% (p. 1736). CRAFT vs Johnson Institute (one trial): 64% (50.45–78.43) vs 30% (15.80–44.20); RR 2.15 (1.28–3.62), P = 0.004, NNT 3 (p. 1733). Family-member change from baseline to 6 months in CRAFT arms (74 CSOs, two trials): depression WMD 3.60 (0.99–6.22), anger 3.39 (1.80–4.99), family cohesion −1.60 (−2.75 to −0.46), relationship happiness −1.28 (−2.16 to −0.39), family conflict 0.94 (0.21–1.67) (p. 1733; Fig 3, p. 1734). No prediction intervals.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The family-member analysis pools only CRAFT arms, and for Meyers et al. (2002) only one of the two CRAFT arms (n = 29), although both were combined for engagement; between-arm comparisons of family-member functioning, which the trials describe as similar, are not pooled. Publication bias is not discussed.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The Johnson comparison rests on one trial of 85 CSOs; the pooled RR rests on 224 CSOs, with Meyers et al. (52.29% of the weight) and Miller et al. (29.97%) carrying most of it.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across four small US trials, relatives whose family members were trained in CRAFT entered treatment about three times as often as when family members received a twelve-step family approach (67% vs 18%; RR 3.25, consistent across trials), and, in the one trial with a Johnson arm, about twice as often (64% vs 30%). Family members' depression, anger and family relationships improved from baseline to 6 months within CRAFT arms; the trials themselves report similar improvement in the comparison arms.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The engagement conclusion matches the pooled data, though 'strong evidence' rests on four small trials, three from CRAFT's originators, without any assessment of publication bias. The abstract says family members showed marked psychosocial and physical improvements whichever approach they received, and the review rates as strong (level 1) the evidence that CRAFT and Al-Anon/Nar-Anon improve family members' functioning (pp. 1729, 1733–1734); the pooled data are before-and-after changes within CRAFT arms with no untreated comparison, which cannot show that any approach caused the improvement, a limitation the authors themselves raise later (p. 1736), and physical symptoms were not pooled. The discussion calls CRAFT almost three times more effective than the Johnson intervention (p. 1736), against the RR of 2.15 on p. 1733. It suggests, without data, that partner violence may also have declined (p. 1735), although the largest alcohol trial excluded families with recent violence (Miller et al., 1999, p. 690). The recommendation that CRAFT be implemented in routine practice (p. 1736) rests on efficacy trials; the one routine-practice study cited engaged 55% (p. 1734).

timeline.event: Sisson and Azrin: 12 female CSOs of male drinkers; 6 of 7 relatives entered treatment with community reinforcement training vs 0 of 5 with the Al-Anon model; therapists crossed with conditions (as described in this review).
Three-arm trial with families of people with alcohol problems: CRAFT 64%, Johnson 30%, Al-Anon facilitation 13% engaged within 6 months
Kirby et al.: 32 CSOs of people using illicit drugs; CRAFT 64% vs Nar-Anon 17% at 10 weeks (as described in this review).
Meyers et al.: 90 CSOs of people using illicit drugs; CRAFT with or without aftercare 67% vs Nar-Anon 29% at 6 months (as described in this review).
Routine-practice effectiveness study of CRAFT: 55% engagement by intention to treat (Dutcher et al., 2009, as described in this review, p. 1734).
This review: CRAFT vs twelve-step family approaches RR 3.25 (2.11–5.02); vs Johnson RR 2.15 from one trial.

replication.where_it_stands: The pooled engagement advantage rests on four small US trials: two from CRAFT's developers, one from the originators of the parent approach, and one (Kirby et al., 1999) with no author in common with the others. Specific rates should be cited from the primary trials, and this review for the pooled relative risk with its limitations. Trials published after November 2008 are not included, and no included trial measured family members' wellbeing against an untreated group.

funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Erasmus University Medical Centre (Rotterdam) and two Dutch addiction services (Novadic-Kentron, Vught; Centrum Maliebaan, Utrecht). The acknowledgements thank R. J. Meyers, J. E. Smith and K. C. Kirby, authors of included trials, for assistance and supplementary data, and the reference list includes a 2009 paper on CRAFT co-written by the first author with Meyers (ref. 39). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: An updated, registered systematic review with duplicate screening and extraction, domain-level risk-of-bias assessment (including investigator allegiance and therapists nested within conditions), discussion of small-study effects, and between-arm rather than before-and-after analyses of family members' wellbeing; and new multi-site trials by independent groups, outside the US, with a usual-care or waiting-list arm.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (CSOs of treatment-resistant adults), intervention (CRAFT), comparators (Al-Anon/Nar-Anon, Johnson Institute) and outcomes (engagement, CSO functioning) are specified.
RCTs and controlled clinical trials were eligible, without an explanation of the choice.

Five databases, keywords given by reference to an earlier review plus listed terms, reference checking and author consultation; no grey literature or trial registries, publication restrictions not stated, and the search is from November 2008.
Not described; only the quality assessment is stated to have been done by two reviewers.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Exclusions are given only as counts by category in the flow diagram (Fig 1); no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives sample size, CSO sex, age, ethnicity and relationship, substances, comparators, follow-up and results; intervention content, settings and recruitment are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: An 11-item internal-validity score (adapted from Cochrane Back Review Group guidelines) was applied by two reviewers independently, but the items and each trial's judgments are not reported, so it cannot be seen whether allocation concealment or blinding was assessed; results are given only as a summary score (all six or more).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: The engagement analysis (random-effects relative risk with heterogeneity tests) is appropriate, but the family-member analysis pools baseline against 6-month scores within CRAFT arms as if they were independent groups, ignoring both the within-person correlation and the randomized comparison arms; it cannot answer the review's own comparative question.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis omitting Sisson & Azrin (1986), the trial flagged for crossing therapists with conditions and for imprecision, left the RR unchanged (3.21); all other trials were rated high quality.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The conclusions call the evidence strong without discussing the trials' risks (unblinded family members, therapists nested within conditions, developers running most trials); the need for an untreated group is noted only in the discussion, while the abstract presents the family-member improvement as a result.
I² = 2.9% for the main analysis; pooling of alcohol and drug trials is discussed and justified by the low heterogeneity.
Not investigated or discussed (with four trials a funnel plot would not be informative, but the possibility is not mentioned).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors declare no interests; funding for the review is not stated, and the acknowledged help from authors of the included trials is not discussed as a potential conflict.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence: five critical items are not met (no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no reported domain-level risk-of-bias assessment, an inappropriate method for the family-member synthesis, risk of bias not used in interpretation) and publication bias is not considered. This judges how far the review's summaries can be trusted, not the trials themselves. The engagement meta-analysis is simple and checkable: its trial-level numbers match the primary trials (for example Miller et al., 1999: 29/45 vs 6/45), heterogeneity is low and the result survives removing the weakest trial. Citable for the pooled engagement relative risk against twelve-step family approaches, with its small, developer-dominated evidence base stated; not for claims that CRAFT or any other approach improves family members' own wellbeing, and not as independent support for the Johnson comparison, which is Miller et al. (1999) alone.

key_findings.finding: Five databases were searched in November 2008; of 245 records (218 after removing duplicates and adding 3), four RCTs met the criteria, with 264 family members in total; all four were rated high quality (six or more of 11 criteria), with 84% agreement between the two reviewers (κ = 0.65).
key_findings.locator: Fig 1 (p. 1730); Methods › Criteria for considering studies and search strategy, 1st paragraph; Results › Study selection and methodological quality, 1st paragraph (p. 1731)
key_findings.note: Record counts are printed only inside the Fig 1 flow diagram (image text, read on the rendered page): 32 + 62 + 94 + 32 + 25 = 245, minus 30 duplicates, plus 3 = 218.

key_findings.finding: Across four trials, relatives entered treatment in 84 of 125 CRAFT cases (67%) against 18 of 99 twelve-step family-approach cases (18%): RR 3.25 (95% CI 2.11–5.02), P < 0.0001, NNT 2, with little heterogeneity (Q = 3.09, df = 3, P = 0.38, I² = 2.9%); graded by the authors as strong evidence (level 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effectiveness of CRAFT versus Al-Anon; Fig 2
key_findings.note: The arm totals (125 and 99) are printed only in the Fig 2 forest plot (image text, read on a rendered crop). The 67% and 18% are simple pooled proportions across trials: an editors' recalculation of Wald intervals from 84/125 and 18/99 reproduces the printed intervals (58.97–75.43 and 10.58–25.78).
Values read from the forest plot on a rendered, rotated 200-dpi crop.

key_findings.finding: Leaving out the smallest trial (Sisson & Azrin, 12 participants) hardly changed the pooled result: RR 3.21 (95% CI 1.99–5.17), NNT 2, I² = 15.3%.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 1735, continues p. 1736)

key_findings.finding: Only one trial (Miller et al., 1999) compared CRAFT with the Johnson Institute intervention: 64% (95% CI 50.45–78.43) vs 30% (15.80–44.20) engaged; RR 2.15 (1.28–3.62), P = 0.004, NNT 3; graded by the authors as limited evidence (level 3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effectiveness of CRAFT versus Johnson Institute intervention

key_findings.finding: The included trials, as summarized: Sisson & Azrin (1986), 12 female CSOs of male drinkers, 86% vs 0% engaged at 3 months; Miller et al. (1999), 130 CSOs of people with alcohol problems, 64% vs 30% vs 13% at 6 months; Kirby et al. (1999), 32 CSOs of people using illicit drugs, 64% vs 17% at 10 weeks; Meyers et al. (2002), 90 CSOs of people using illicit drugs, two CRAFT arms combined 67% vs 29% at 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of included studies, 1st–4th paragraphs (p. 1731); Table 1 (p. 1732)

key_findings.finding: Family members' functioning: within the CRAFT arms of two trials (74 CSOs), scores improved from baseline to 6 months for depression (WMD 3.60, 95% CI 0.99–6.22), anger (3.39, 1.80–4.99), family cohesion (−1.60, −2.75 to −0.46), relationship happiness (−1.28, −2.16 to −0.39) and family conflict (0.94, 0.21–1.67); the review states that family members in the Al-Anon/Nar-Anon and Johnson arms improved similarly, whether or not the relative entered treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results › CSO improvements, 1st paragraph (begins p. 1733, continues p. 1734); Fig 3 (p. 1734)
key_findings.note: These are before-and-after changes within CRAFT arms, not comparisons between randomized arms; the authors later say a no-treatment group is needed to rule out change that would occur anyway (Limitations, 5th paragraph, p. 1736).

key_findings.finding: The authors summarize that CRAFT gets about two-thirds of relatives who refused treatment to attend it, and that engagement typically came after four to six CRAFT sessions with the family member.

Studies outside the meta-analysis, as cited by the review: an uncontrolled CRAFT study of 62 family members of people who used drugs, 74% engaged; a routine-practice effectiveness study, 55% engaged by intention to treat; parents of adolescents, 71% engaged; and unpublished data, as personal communications, of 40% engagement with a self-help book or self-directed treatment and 70% with a group format.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Clinical implications, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 1734–1735); Limitations, 6th paragraph (p. 1736)
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures from studies not appraised here.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the quality assessment was not checked with the trial authors; alcohol and drug trials were pooled; the smallest trial was imprecise; which CRAFT components work is unknown; and an untreated comparison group is needed for the family-member outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The family-member meta-analysis (Fig 3) treats baseline and 6-month scores of the same CRAFT participants as two independent groups ('Favours baseline' against 'Favours 6 months'), ignores the randomized comparison arms, uses only one of the two CRAFT arms of Meyers et al. (n = 29) although both were combined for engagement, and assumes n = 45 at both times for Miller et al.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled 'improvements' describe change over time in CRAFT arms; they cannot be attributed to CRAFT, and their intervals do not account for the paired design. Miller et al. (1999, p. 694) report no difference between arms in these measures.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says CRAFT was found almost three times more effective than the Johnson Institute intervention (p. 1736), while the results report RR 2.15 and describe CRAFT as two times more effective (p. 1733).
reporting_issues.consequence: The discussion overstates the only comparison with the Johnson intervention.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says family members showed marked psychosocial and physical improvements in all three approaches, but no physical-symptom outcome was pooled, and the pooled analyses are within CRAFT arms only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract presents an untested, uncontrolled improvement as a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says CRAFT encouraged about two-thirds of relatives to attend treatment 'typically for four to six CRAFT sessions', which reads as if the relatives attended four to six sessions; the body says engagement occurred after four to six CRAFT sessions with the family member (p. 1735).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the four to six sessions are the family member's, not the relative's.

reporting_issues.issue: The Fig 3 legend calls the depression measure the BDI-II, while Miller et al. (1999, p. 690) cite the original Beck Depression Inventory (Beck, Steer & Garbin, 1988).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the instrument version is mislabelled for at least one trial.
